outcome: Since 26 Jan 2024 the three-dimensional case was proved by Wang and Zahl (preprint 24 Feb 2025, not journal-accepted as far as found) and restated in a streamlined proof by Guth, Wang and Zahl (Jan 2026); on 6 Oct 2026 OpenAI posted, in an unreviewed GitHub release, a preprint dated 24 Sep 2026 claiming that every subset of R^4 containing a unit segment in every direction has Hausdorff dimension 4, with no Lean proof and no independent check found; the general conjecture for n >= 5 remains open.
problem_asks: Two claims, each asserted for every dimension n. (a) Hausdorff dimension: a set E in R^n that contains a unit line segment in every direction has Hausdorff dimension n. (b) Minkowski dimension: the same sets have Minkowski dimension n. The statement is the conjunction of (a) and (b) over all n (Wikipedia wording: do n-dimensional sets that contain a unit line segment in every direction necessarily have Hausdorff dimension and Minkowski dimension equal to n?). The statement places no compactness, boundedness or measurability hypothesis on E, and gives no convention for the Minkowski dimension of unbounded sets. n = 1 is trivial; n = 2 is classical; the question is open for n >= 3 as posed, with n = 3 since settled by Wang and Zahl (2025) for both parts.

events.what_happened: Roy Davies, 'Some remarks on the Kakeya problem' (1971), settles the planar case: Kakeya sets in R^2 have Hausdorff dimension 2. Credited for the planar case in the current Wikipedia article 'Kakeya set' and listed in the bibliography of the OpenAI 4D manuscript. The paper itself was not opened; the venue is not verified.
events.delivers: n = 2 only: Hausdorff dimension 2 for planar Kakeya sets.
events.remains: Every n >= 3, both the Hausdorff and the Minkowski part.
events.time_since_posted: over 50 years; treated as settled in the literature
events.direction: Positive for the conjecture, but only for n = 2.

events.what_happened: Tom Wolff, 'An improved bound for Kakeya type maximal functions' (1995), gives the lower bound (n+2)/2 for the dimension of Kakeya sets in R^n (Wikipedia, opened); Quanta (Mar 2025) reports the 1995 result that no Kakeya set in R^3 has dimension below 2.5. Paper not opened.
events.delivers: Partial lower bound (n+2)/2 for every n, in particular 2.5 for n = 3.
events.remains: Equality (dimension n) for every n >= 3, both parts.
events.direction: Partial; points toward the conjecture but falls short of it.

Per the arXiv search snippet, the Minkowski dimension of Besicovitch sets in R^3 is at least 5/2 plus a fixed positive constant. Not opened; described from search results only.

events.remains: Full dimension 3 in R^3 (later settled by Wang and Zahl, 2025) and all n >= 4.
events.direction: Partial; toward the conjecture in R^3 but short of it.

events.direction: Partial; toward the conjecture but short of it.

events.what_happened: OpenAI, 'Every four-dimensional Kakeya set has full Hausdorff dimension' (paper dated 24 Sep 2026), posted to the openai/math repository; the repository's first and only commit ('Initial commit', adc7f12) is dated 6 Oct 2026, the first public appearance I could evidence. The abstract, from the paper's LaTeX source: 'We prove the four-dimensional Hausdorff-dimension Kakeya conjecture: every subset of R^4 containing a unit line segment in every direction has Hausdorff dimension four. No compactness or regularity assumption is imposed on the set or its witnessing line family.' Theorem 1 (Section 1, read from the LaTeX): 'Let K subset R^4. Suppose that for every e in S^3 there is a point a_e in R^4 such that {a_e + t e : 0 <= t <= 1} subset K. Then dim_H K = 4.' Section 1.1: 'If the set is bounded, both its lower and upper Minkowski dimensions are four.' Section 1.2: every Kakeya set in R^d, d >= 4, has dim_H >= 4, 'in particular, this holds in dimension five', and 'the full conjecture in R^d asks for dimension d'. Section 1.4 claims Nikodym sets in R^4 (resolving Conjecture 1.4 of Gao-Liu-Xi in dimension four). The paper does not claim the four-dimensional Kakeya maximal conjecture. Its reduction uses the companion 3D manuscript's Lemma 2.3.
events.revisions: Paper's own date 24 Sep 2026; one commit (6 Oct 2026); whether it was among the 14 manuscripts revised on 7 Oct 2026 is not established.
events.delivers: (a) Hausdorff part at n = 4, for all subsets of R^4 containing a unit segment in every direction, with no compactness or measurability hypothesis (Theorem 1). (b) Minkowski part at n = 4 for bounded sets only (Section 1.1). Dimension 5 and higher: only the weaker lower bound dim_H >= 4 (Section 1.2). The paper does not state a Minkowski result for unbounded sets in R^4.
events.remains: Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension d for every d >= 5 (open per the paper's own statement); the Minkowski part for unbounded sets in R^4 (not stated in the parts read).
events.time_since_posted: 6 days (6 Oct 2026 to 12 Oct 2026); no expert engagement with the argument found

A third-party tracker (VibeMathed, not authoritative) records 'Verification: Unreviewed' and 'No independent mathematician has checked this yet' and 'The proof was not refereed'. Scientific American (8 Oct 2026) says no one had yet been able to read through the release. (2) No Lean proof for this paper (GitHub issue google-deepmind/formal-conjectures #6910, 7 Oct 2026: 'No Lean proof is included in the release for this paper'). The release README says results are at 'different stages of verification' and that 'Some of the unformalized results could have issues'. (3) Dependency: the reduction uses Lemma 2.3 of the companion 3D manuscript (weighted full-time plank bound), itself unreviewed and unformalised. (4) Batch context: three other OpenAI manuscripts (Weil classes on split abelian eightfolds; Kuga-Satake for K3 surfaces; rational Hodge for products of K3 surfaces) were withdrawn on 7 Oct 2026 for a sign error that invalidated linked arguments; OpenAI said roughly half the results were released unconfirmed (Retraction Watch, 8 Oct 2026). This paper is not among the withdrawn (kingy.ai; family 074). (5) The model is unreleased and the per-paper procedure is not described. (6) I read the abstract, Theorem 1 and the corollaries in Sections 1 and 10 only, not the proof in Sections 2 to 9.

disputes.summary: Two claims on the three-dimensional Kakeya maximal conjecture: Rios and Sawyer v1 (26 Jun 2025) claimed a proof and was withdrawn in v2 (2 Jul 2025); OpenAI's companion manuscript (paper dated 23 Sep 2026, public 6 Oct 2026) reportedly proves the stronger maximal form, unreviewed. No resolution found. Both concern the maximal statement at n = 3, not the bullet's set statement.

The OpenAI 4D manuscript and its companion credit 'OpenAI' alone. The release README says most results came from an unreleased internal OpenAI model. Neither paper states what the model did. The 'solved' wording in Scientific American and the Wikipedia article reports the claim as a settled result, while the GitHub issue and the release's own caveats describe it as unverified.

One search summary said the 36kr report claims Lean formalisation of the OpenAI 4D result. The 36kr page as read says 'This result has no formalization', and the formal-conjectures issue says no Lean proof is included. The record treats the 4D result as unformalised.

A search summary attributed to the Epoch arithmetic Kakeya page a GPT-5.2 Pro solution of the warm-up variant and a Gemini 3 Deep Think non-solution. The page as fetched twice names no AI model and gives no attempt status. Unresolved; not recorded as an event.

summary: The n = 3 case has been proved, and the n = 4 Hausdorff case is claimed by OpenAI, but nothing has settled n >= 5. Wang and Zahl's preprint (arXiv 2502.17655, 24 Feb 2025, 127 pp.) proves that every Kakeya set in R^3 has Minkowski and Hausdorff dimension 3. I read its HTML to within about 10,000 characters of the end: no AI, Lean or computer-assistance mention, and the Acknowledgements name no AI system. The record shows v1 only and no journal reference as of 12 Oct 2026; the authors' 2022 sticky-case companion is listed in J. Amer. Math. Soc. 39 (2026). A streamlined proof by Guth, Wang and Zahl (arXiv 2601.14411, 20 Jan 2026) was read in full. Expository work (Tao's blog, 25 Feb 2025; Guth's surveys of May 2025, Aug 2025 and Apr 2026) sketches the argument; none of it is a verification statement, and Guth's April survey says not all steps can be sketched. The Lean benchmark statement (lean-eval) uses sorry. A Hua-Yang paper (Aug 2026) describes a 'conditional' Kakeya input and a companion's reference list names a 'conditional repair of the streamlined three-dimensional Kakeya reduction'; I read only the abstract and did not establish what the gap is. Earlier partial results are recorded as events: Davies (plane, 1971), Wolff ((n+2)/2, 1995), Katz-Laba-Tao (1999), Katz-Tao (2001), Katz-Zahl (R^4 at 3.059, Feb 2019), Hickman-Rogers-Zhang (2019), Wang-Zahl (sticky R^3, 2022), Rai Choudhuri (sticky R^4 at 3.25, Oct 2024) and Borges et al. (R^4 Kakeya maximal estimate at 3.054, Nov 2025). The central new event is OpenAI's preprint 'Every four-dimensional Kakeya set has full Hausdorff dimension' (paper dated 24 Sep 2026; first public on 6 Oct 2026 in the openai/math repository). Its abstract and Theorem 1 claim dim_H K = 4 for every K in R^4 containing a unit segment in every direction, with no compactness or measurability hypothesis; Section 1.1 gives both Minkowski dimensions equal to 4 for bounded such sets. Its reduction uses Lemma 2.3 of a companion OpenAI manuscript on the 3D Kakeya maximal conjecture, also unreviewed. No Lean proof exists for either. I found no expert engagement with the argument and no erratum or withdrawal as of 12 Oct 2026. The three manuscripts withdrawn on 7 Oct 2026 (Weil classes, Kuga-Satake, rational Hodge) are not Kakeya papers. The AI attribution rests on the repository README's general statement that 'the vast majority of results' came from 'an unreleased internal OpenAI model'. The Kakeya paper itself credits 'OpenAI' alone and says nothing about production, and no per-paper method is given, so I cannot say what the model did for this proof. AlphaEvolve, Deep Think and AlphaProof did produce finite-field Kakeya and Nikodym constructions (Nov 2025) and numerical bounds for arithmetic and planar variants; these are real AI-involved Kakeya events, but they answer different questions and are recorded as such. Close calls: (a) I date the OpenAI event to its 6 Oct public appearance, not the 24 Sep paper date, because the repository's only commit is 6 Oct; (b) the Minkowski part for n = 4 is supported only for bounded sets, as the corollary is stated; (c) the 3D companion is cited for a lemma that the 4D argument depends on, which I did not read; (d) Hua-Yang's 'conditional repair' may or may not touch the 2025 original. Hong Wang received the 2026 Fields Medal (IMU, 23 Jul 2026, per the Simons Foundation listing in search results) for this work; the citation text was not retrieved, and I treat the medal as a recognition, not an event.
competing_reading: The OpenAI 4D theorem is an unconditional statement with a clean hypothesis-free formulation, and its abstract says it proves the four-dimensional Hausdorff conjecture; read at face value it settles the Hausdorff part at n = 4 and, for bounded sets, the Minkowski part at n = 4. On that reading the open part is n >= 5 alone. The opposing reading: an unreviewed, unformalised preprint from a batch where three manuscripts were withdrawn within a day for a sign error; where its reduction depends on an unreviewed companion lemma; where the authors describe the release as partly unconfirmed; and where no qualified reader has engaged. On that reading n = 4 is not yet established and the Minkowski part is not established even for bounded sets. A third reading applies to the 3D base: the Wang-Zahl argument, which the 4D paper cites as its foundation, has not been journal-accepted in the sources I found, and the conditional Hua-Yang repair suggests part of the streamlined version needs an extra hypothesis.
what_would_settle_it: For the OpenAI 4D result: a referee-level or expert written assessment of Sections 2 to 9 and of Lemma 2.3 in the companion 3D manuscript; a Lean formalisation of Theorem 1 and of the companion lemma; a public erratum, a withdrawal, or a citing paper that relies on the result; and the authors' own account of how the proof was found. For the Minkowski part at n = 4, the paper's treatment of unbounded sets. For the 3D base: a journal acceptance or an independent write-up of the Wang-Zahl proof, and a resolution of the Hua-Yang 'conditional repair' (what hypothesis, and whether it affects the 2025 or the 2026 version). For n >= 5 nothing short of a new proof or a counterexample would change the status.
